A widow. The Sema writes that the same applies to a divorced woman, and the Taz adds that the same applies to an unmarried woman. I say that once we begin adding categories to what the Torah expressly stated, there is no end. I too could say that if a woman's husband traveled overseas and she is left alone, one should not take collateral from her, for all the more so might repeated visits give her a bad reputation among her neighbors while she remains a married woman. But Heaven forbid that we alter even the smallest detail of the Torah's wording. The central point is that a widow's tears are upon her cheeks and she weeps over her broken state. In our sins, her condition resembles the destruction of our glorious House. See Ramban to Parashat Mishpatim on the verse "you shall not afflict any widow," where he explains that the Torah had special compassion for a widow, and Hashem is close to the brokenhearted. Therefore the first Tanna holds that one may not take collateral from any widow. Rabbi Shimon holds that if this special compassion were the sole consideration, we should likewise refrain from collecting from her property altogether. Rather, with respect to monetary collection itself we do not extend the exemption. The prohibition is because the repeated taking and returning of collateral may create a bad reputation among her neighbors, causing renewed anguish and tears. The Torah was especially solicitous of the widow's grief in that circumstance. But Heaven forbid that we add other categories to the verse. This is especially true of a divorced woman, concerning whom the Torah permits the husband to remove the marital bond. How can we invent a new exemption out of compassion that the Torah did not state? Rabbi Shimon himself did not uproot the verse from its plain meaning. He interpreted "the garment of a widow" as referring to a poor widow whose garment is her only covering. Indeed, Riaz holds that only her clothing may not be taken as collateral. In any event, one must not depart from the verse's meaning or add a category that Chazal did not receive and derive through the thirteen interpretive principles transmitted to them, with the spirit of Hashem within them. See Shach, seif katan 1.
Not at the time of the loan. The Rambam writes that taking collateral from a widow is prohibited even at the time of the loan, while many authorities disagree. The Maggid Mishneh brings proof for the dissenting view from Rabbi Shimon, who explains the prohibition as preventing the creditor from giving the widow a bad reputation among her neighbors. That concern does not apply to collateral taken at the moment of the loan, because the law of periodic return does not apply there. From Rabbi Shimon, the Maggid Mishneh infers the same limit for the first Tanna, since they need not be assumed to dispute that separate issue. According to his reasoning, when he states categorically that collateral taken at the time of the loan is not subject to periodic return, this must mean only in the absence of the special prohibition. The Rambam himself writes that if one did take the widow's garment he must return it against his will, meaning at the time of her need, as the Sema explains and as stated above. The fact that lashes apply only if the item was lost or burned likewise shows that the prohibition is redirected to the positive command of return. The Maggid Mishneh's intent must therefore be that since the Torah prohibited taking this collateral, although ordinarily the transaction would have been effective, Scripture imposed a duty to return it when needed. Had the Torah not prohibited the taking in the first place, there would have been no basis for applying the law of periodic return to this collateral. Thus one may ask why the Torah should prohibit it at the time of the loan and thereby create a return obligation when, absent that prohibition, there would be no repeated visits and no bad reputation. This is the Maggid Mishneh's proof. Even so, his argument is not clear to me. The Ramah, cited by the Rama in this seif, holds that one may not take food preparation implements as collateral from a guarantor. This indicates that the exclusion derived from "you shall not enter his house," which allows entry into the house of a guarantor, concerns only the prohibition on entering the debtor's house, while the separate prohibition "you shall not take the millstones" is not excluded and applies even to a guarantor. If so, the same should be true of "you shall not take a widow's garment." Since the permission to enter a guarantor's house does not eliminate other collateral prohibitions, a widow who is a guarantor would still be protected. The difficulty according to Rabbi Shimon remains. He bases the prohibition on the concern for a bad reputation. Yet according to the Tur's position, cited later, collateral taken from a guarantor is not subject to periodic return. If a widow serves as guarantor, Rabbi Shimon's rationale would permit taking her collateral, while the first Tanna would prohibit it. That would create a new dispute between them not mentioned by the Gemara. Likewise, if a woman owes money to another woman, Rabbi Shimon's concern for suspicion of immoral conduct may not apply. The same would be true if a son takes collateral from his mother. Rabbi Shimon would permit these cases while the first Tanna would prohibit them, again creating new disputes. It therefore appears clear that all of these cases are included in the single dispute itself. In his commentary to the Mishnah, the Rambam explains the first Tanna's reason: taking collateral from a widow cannot avoid producing some dispute or interaction that may generate suspicion or other harm. Rabbi Shimon holds that the concern applies only where the collateral must repeatedly be returned. Thus the Gemara's terms "wealthy" and "poor" are classifications of whether the law of return applies. A wealthy widow represents every case where there is no duty of periodic return, including a guarantor or collateral taken at the time of the loan. A poor widow represents every case where periodic return applies. The first Tanna prohibits even where there is no return obligation, while Rabbi Shimon limits the prohibition to situations involving return. It is all one dispute, and this is clear. The Maggid Mishneh's formulation is therefore not fully persuasive to me. The Rambam's own explanation also requires clarification. He writes that the reason is that taking collateral from a widow cannot avoid conflict and dealings that may cause her a bad reputation. Yet the Gemara says that Rabbi Shimon is the one who interprets the rationale of the verse, implying that the first Tanna does not base his ruling upon a stated rationale. The Lechem Mishneh already raises this difficulty, noting that the Gemara compares the dispute to Rabbi Shimon's treatment of the prohibition against a king multiplying wives. It seems that the Rambam understands the dispute about interpreting the reason of a verse in a more precise way. Certainly no mitzvah is without a reason. The Rambam explains in Moreh Nevuchim that the reasons of many mitzvot operate according to the majority of cases. There can be exceptional cases to which the reason does not apply, but the Torah legislates according to the general rule. This is the position of the authority who does not derive legal exceptions from the reason of the verse. Once the rationale applies to the majority, we do not exempt the minority merely because that rationale is absent there. The Rambam's explanation that conflict cannot always be avoided does not literally apply to every widow and every form of collateral. If a person takes a specified item from a modest woman under a clear written agreement witnessed by others, there may be no conflict or suspicion whatsoever. Nevertheless, because the first Tanna does not derive exceptions from the rationale, the Torah's prohibition applies to all widows once its purpose generally applies in most cases. Rabbi Shimon, however, does derive law from the reason of the verse. If he can identify a category to which the stated concern does not apply, he excludes that category from the prohibition. He therefore reasons that Scripture's phrase "the garment of a widow" refers specifically to a poor widow whose garment is her only covering and who is entitled to repeated return of the pledge. In such a case every widow is exposed to the concern of a bad reputation because the creditor repeatedly comes to return and reclaim the garment. A wealthy widow, where no return is required, is excluded. The same model applies to a king multiplying wives. Even righteous women such as Abigail would not turn his heart away, but most wives may do so, and "a woman of valor, who can find." The first Tanna therefore applies the general prohibition to all additional wives. Rabbi Shimon, who interprets the rationale as defining the law, permits the exceptional case where the concern does not apply. This resolves the matter.
If she denies, etc. See what I wrote in Urim explaining the Rivash. His interpretation is strained, and Baal HaTerumot, sha'ar 49, part 4, law 26, does not understand the Rambam that way. After proving from the Gemara's case of the man who seized a knife, which was an implement used for food preparation, that the creditor nevertheless has a migo that he could have denied the seizure entirely or claimed that he returned it, Baal HaTerumot proceeds to clarify the law of one who takes a widow's garment. He writes that it appears equivalent to the law of a food preparation implement, since there is no basis to distinguish them. Yet the Rambam writes concerning a widow that if she admits, she pays, and if she denies, she swears. Baal HaTerumot therefore understood the Rambam differently from the Rivash, and that the Rambam stated this rule specifically in the case of a widow. This is difficult, because the Rivash's explanation is exceedingly strained. According to Baal HaTerumot's understanding of the Rambam, perhaps the Rambam is speaking of a wealthy widow, from whom the creditor is not presently obligated to return the pledge. When the Rambam says that he must return it against his will, this means only when it later becomes needed if she becomes poor, as explained above. Before that time there is no obligation to return. The case could therefore be one where the creditor took the pledge in the presence of witnesses but there were no witnesses who continuously observed it. Ordinarily he would have a migo that he returned it. Here, however, such a migo is unavailable, because there is no present obligation to return it and the situation resembles a debt that is not yet due. Since the creditor deliberately violated the prohibition and took a widow's pledge in order to retain security, why should we assume that he returned it when there was no reason to do so? The migo is therefore weak. Even according to the authority who accepts a migo against a chazakah, this may be a particularly strong chazakah. Alternatively, since the pledge remains presumptively the widow's property, the creditor is the one seeking to collect through it and therefore certainly cannot rely on a migo without an oath. This would explain why the Rambam stated the rule in the case of a widow, whereas a food preparation implement is subject to return. In truth, however, all the commentators write that the Rambam began with a widow merely because she was the first case under discussion, but his language governs all the prohibited pledges mentioned afterward. Moreover, the suggested reading that his unqualified statement refers only to a wealthy widow is strained. There is another possible explanation based on the Rambam's general position that one who committed robbery in the presence of witnesses must return the stolen property in the presence of witnesses. The Maggid Mishneh understands this to be the Rambam's view, and the Mabit and his son Maharit explain the rationale: because the offender committed the theft openly and thereby established himself as a wrongdoer, when he returns the property he must do so before witnesses in order to establish that he corrected the wrong. According to this, one who forcibly seizes a food preparation implement or the like is certainly a full robber. As the Shach writes, everyone agrees that in such a case he bears liability even for unavoidable loss. He therefore resembles one who robbed in the presence of witnesses and must return in the presence of witnesses. Indeed, that rule itself is stated concerning the famous case of Rabbi Abba's ingot. The authorities who adopt it hold that even though there were no witnesses who continuously saw the object, the defendant has no migo that he returned it, because the original snatching occurred before witnesses. The same would apply here. There would be no migo unless the pledge was taken at the time of the loan. The Rambam holds that even taking a widow's garment or a food preparation implement at the time of the loan violates a prohibition, but since the debtor voluntarily delivered it, the creditor is not technically a robber. Still, the same rationale for requiring witnessed return may apply. Since he openly violated the prohibition by taking the widow's garment, his eventual return is the act that repairs his wrongdoing, and he should establish that return before witnesses. He therefore lacks the migo of having returned it. The Gemara's case involving Rava's seizure of a knife must then have involved no witnesses at all, so that the defendant retained the migo that the seizure never occurred. The difficulty with this explanation is that the Shulchan Aruch should not have copied the Rambam's ruling without qualification, because as explained above in siman 90 and below in the laws of robbery, the Mechaber does not rule that one who steals in the presence of witnesses must also return in the presence of witnesses. Therefore. One of two explanations must be adopted. The first is that the Rambam is not discussing admission and denial of the underlying debt at all. That is an independent matter, and it is obvious that the creditor cannot collect a disputed debt without proof. Rather, the debt itself is clearly established by witnesses or a document. The Rambam says that the creditor must return the forbidden pledge, and the parties dispute whether he in fact returned it. The creditor says that he returned the pledge, while the widow denies receiving it. Although the creditor holds the debt instrument, because it is known that he took collateral and they dispute its return, the borrower is believed with an oath that the pledge was not returned, and the creditor loses the amount represented by the pledge. Thus, "if she admits" means that she admits he returned the pledge and she must pay, while "if she denies" means that she denies return, swears, and thereby defeats his collection. This accords with the Tur's ruling below in seif 21 in the name of Rabbi Yosef ibn Plat. See what I write there. The second possibility is that the Rambam follows the Geonim who hold that a creditor who asserts, "the pledge is worth only this amount of my debt," and relies on a migo, is one of those who swear and collect. He therefore requires the oath imposed by the Mishnah, as in the case of one who rents utensils and the like. This is well known. The Rambam rules above in siman 84 and siman 92 that whenever a person who ordinarily swears and collects is disqualified from taking an oath, the opposing party swears and is exempt. A creditor who violated a Torah prohibition by taking forbidden collateral becomes suspect and cannot take the Mishnah's oath. He therefore loses the benefit of his migo, and the opposing party swears and is exempt. This is a significant novelty in the Rambam: even though the creditor would otherwise have a migo, if the widow denies liability she herself swears and is exempt because he is disqualified from swearing. As for Rava's case, either there were no witnesses to the unlawful seizure, and a person does not become disqualified merely by his own admission of wrongdoing, or, according to the view above that the opposing litigant may still say, "you admitted that you are disqualified, so I will swear instead," the seizure there was inadvertent. Tosafot explain that the entire incident occurred through error because the creditor did not know that taking a food preparation implement was prohibited. He therefore was not rendered suspect. "Who can understand errors?" This explanation appears correct as practical law.
If the pledge was lost or burned, he receives lashes. The Rambam writes this concerning one who takes a widow's garment and one who takes a food preparation implement, and also concerning a creditor who enters the debtor's house to seize collateral. In the first two cases, however, he does not say that the creditor calculates the value of the pledge and then claims the balance of the debt. In the case of entry into the debtor's house, he does write that the creditor calculates the pledge's value. This is strong proof for the Shach's position that where the creditor entered the debtor's house and forcibly took the pledge, his liability for unavoidable loss arises because he is a robber. He acquires liability for the object and becomes responsible even for accidents. By contrast, the first two cases include collateral taken at the time of the loan with the debtor's consent. There the creditor is not a robber and has no general liability for unavoidable loss, so the Rambam does not say that he deducts the pledge's value from the debt. One may add that according to the view above in siman 72 that Rabbi Yosef's perutah benefit for a pledge does not arise from the duty to air and care for it, but specifically at the moment of the loan when the lender performs a mitzvah and is thereby exempt from giving a coin to a poor person, even that rationale may not apply here. A lender who is simultaneously violating a Torah prohibition by taking forbidden collateral cannot claim the mitzvah benefit as the basis for acquiring greater responsibility. His gain is offset by his transgression. The commentators challenge the Rambam's ruling from the Gemara in Makkot. The Gemara says that because the creditor is liable to pay for the pledge, the prohibition remains one redirected to a positive command, or alternatively that one cannot both receive lashes and make payment. The matter can be resolved according to our text and Tosafot's explanation that the payment obligation preserves the corrective character of the command. Asifat Zekenim cites Tosafot of Sens, who answer Tosafot's question about why one who takes the upper and lower millstones can receive two sets of lashes despite the apparent positive command of return. They write that the payment obligation does not necessarily repair the prohibition. The creditor may simply deduct the value of the destroyed millstones from the outstanding debt. He is not obligated to hand the debtor money with which to buy replacement millstones so that the debtor can again prepare food. Whether the creditor retains the original pledge or merely retains its value through setoff, the debtor has still lost an implement needed for his livelihood. In that sense, the duty of return has not been fulfilled. This is an excellent conceptual point, but the commentators object that the Gemara in Makkot itself says that because the creditor is liable for payment, the prohibition remains corrected through the positive command. The answer must be that according to Rava, who holds that any act performed contrary to the Torah is ineffective, where Scripture commanded return and the creditor deliberately defeats that command by destroying or selling the pledge, his attempt to frustrate the Torah's instruction cannot be legally effective. He must therefore use the value to procure a replacement food implement so that the return command can still be fulfilled. It is possible that even Abaye would agree in this setting, because otherwise every person could evade the corrective command by selling or breaking the pledge. At least according to Rava, however, this is certain. That reasoning applies where the creditor himself deliberately destroys the pledge. If an accident occurs and he merely becomes monetarily liable because, as a robber, he bears responsibility for accidents, he did not perform any new prohibited act designed to defeat the Torah's command. Rava's rule that an unlawful act is ineffective therefore has no application. It is enough that the pledge's value is deducted from the debt, and the creditor need not purchase another implement. Ramban in Milchamot Hashem, in the chapter Shevuat HaDayanim, writes that the Makkot sugya follows the authority who holds that lashes depend upon actively nullifying the positive command. Even according to the Shach's reading of the Rambam that liability for the pledge can exist according to the authority who focuses on whether the positive command was fulfilled, because the creditor acquired accident liability, the Rambam must in any event interpret the Gemara in light of the distinction between active nullification and mere failure of fulfillment. The Rambam holds that taking a widow's garment or a food preparation implement at the time of the loan also violates the prohibition and is redirected to a positive command. Yet if such consensually delivered collateral is accidentally lost, the creditor is not liable for accidents, as explained above. The Gemara's inability to find a case of lashes therefore necessarily follows the authority who requires active nullification, because an accidental loss is not active nullification. Accordingly, the Rambam can adopt Tosafot of Sens. Where the pledge is accidentally lost or burned and we rule according to the authority who considers failure to fulfill the command sufficient for lashes, the creditor receives lashes because merely deducting the value from the debt is not actual return. By contrast, the Makkot sugya follows the authority who requires active nullification. Its case is one where the creditor himself burns or destroys the pledge. In that case Rava's rule makes the deliberate frustration ineffective, so the creditor must replace the item and the positive command can still be fulfilled. The Gemara therefore says that payment keeps the prohibition within the corrective framework. This resolves Tosafot's question concerning the Mishnah's statement that one can receive two or three sets of lashes for taking forbidden collateral. There is no need to say that the prohibitions are not redirected to a positive command, which would create the earlier difficulty why the Gemara in Temurah does not identify these cases as differences between Abaye and Rava. The Mishnah can follow the authority who holds that failure to fulfill the corrective command generates lashes, and the Rambam understands that standard differently from Tosafot in Makkot. For the Rambam, the person does not receive lashes merely because beit din warned him to return the pledge and he delayed. Lashes apply only when fulfillment has become impossible, such as where the pledge was accidentally burned. So long as return remains possible, there are no lashes. This also answers the Kesef Mishneh's question in Hilchot Shechitah, chapter 13, why the Rambam rules according to the authority who focuses on fulfillment rather than active nullification, since Rabbi Yochanan appears to hold the latter view. The entire dispute between Abaye and Rava about whether unlawful acts take effect fits naturally with the authority who focuses on fulfillment, and halachah follows their analysis, which supports the alternative ruling. It is even more likely, however, that the Rambam had the older text of Makkot recorded by Rivash and other authorities. According to that text, the Gemara answers simply that since monetary payment applies, we do not impose both lashes and payment. That reading is preferable. The version that calls the payment itself fulfillment of the positive command is difficult in light of Tosafot of Sens, because the creditor is not literally required to buy a replacement implement. The older text was apparently also the Raavad's version, as suggested by his gloss. Tosafot ask that if both lashes and payment are available, we ordinarily say that the offender receives lashes and does not pay. But that principle applies where Scripture has not otherwise revealed a preference for monetary restoration. Here the Torah explicitly reveals that it wants restoration by redirecting the prohibition to "you shall surely return it." Once the corrective command can no longer be performed, payment is therefore more appropriate than lashes. This resembles the rule that Scripture specially increased the liability of false witnesses toward monetary payment. Here too Scripture indicated its preference for restoring the debtor's loss. This is especially compelling according to what was explained that the creditor who forcibly seized the pledge is a robber. A robber ordinarily pays rather than receiving lashes, and it would be unreasonable for the borrower to lose the value of his pledge merely because the creditor receives corporal punishment. Now. Rashi explains the dispute between "he fulfilled it or did not fulfill it" and "he nullified it or did not nullify it" as follows. According to the first view, the prohibition is violated immediately, so a warning can take effect at the moment of the act and is not merely a doubtful warning. Although the offender may later perform the corrective command, until he does so the prohibition remains operative and the warning attaches. According to the second view, liability depends upon a later act of nullification. Until the person actively destroys the possibility of correction, the original prohibition does not ripen into lashes. The warning is therefore initially uncertain. This distinction yields another practical difference. Liability to pay for the pledge arises only when the pledge is lost or burned. Tosafot and the other authorities explain this in the discussion of a borrowed and rented animal: the obligation crystallizes at the time of the loss, which is why a person may be uncertain whether the item was borrowed or rented in a manner analogous to one who does not know whether he ever incurred a loan. According to the view that liability to lashes depends upon failure to fulfill the positive command, the prohibition and warning attach from the original unlawful taking, while the monetary obligation arises only later when the pledge is destroyed. Lashes and payment therefore do not arise simultaneously, and the rule that one punishment excludes the other does not apply. The Maggid Mishneh makes precisely this point, that the liabilities do not arise at one moment. According to the view that lashes require active nullification, by contrast, the essential liability to lashes arises only when the offender destroys the pledge and thereby nullifies the corrective command. At that exact moment the monetary obligation for the pledge also arises. Lashes and payment therefore coincide, and the familiar rule that one who pays does not receive lashes, or one who receives lashes does not pay, becomes directly relevant. This explains why the Makkot sugya, which proceeds according to the active-nullification view, answers through the monetary liability. According to our ruling based on failure of fulfillment, the two liabilities arise at different times, so the Rambam can hold that the creditor both pays and receives lashes. This also makes the dispute between Abaye and Rava fit the authority who focuses on fulfillment. Nor is there any difficulty from the Mishnah stating that one who takes the millstones violates two separate prohibitions. According to what was explained, the absence of lashes in the Makkot discussion results only from the principle that payment and lashes coincide. The Mishnah can follow Rabbi Meir, as anonymous Mishnayot often do, and Rabbi Meir holds that a person can both pay and receive lashes. There is therefore no difficulty. This entire explanation is clear, and it removes the need to assume that the Rambam possessed a different text, as the Maggid Mishneh suggested.
Some say that nevertheless, with respect to taking food preparation implements as collateral, etc. This is somewhat difficult. If so, what is the Gemara's question against Shmuel, who holds that even an agent of beit din may not enter the debtor's house? Scripture says, "he shall not take the millstones as collateral," and likewise, "he shall not take a widow's garment." The Gemara infers that other items may be taken. Why not say that these separate prohibitions are needed specifically in cases where taking ordinary collateral is otherwise permitted, such as from a guarantor and the like? If the Maharshal's interpretation were sustainable, that the baraita itself should be read as expressly implying "other items may be taken," the difficulty could be resolved because the contradiction would arise from the baraita rather than from the verse. But Maharsha rejects that reading forcefully, and his position is correct. Suppose the Ramah held that a guarantor and similar persons are not subject to the mitzvah of returning a pledge, because the command of return is attached to the prohibition "you shall not enter his house," whereas that prohibition is relaxed with respect to a guarantor, as the Tur writes later. Then another problem arises. According to Rava, who holds that an act done in violation of the Torah is ineffective, one who takes a forbidden food implement from a guarantor should have to return it immediately. One could not say that the prohibition was redirected to a positive command, because the return command would not apply to a guarantor. Nor can one say that this really is the law, because then the Gemara in Temurah should have listed this as a practical difference between Abaye and Rava. One would have to answer that the prohibition against taking food preparation implements also applies to an ordinary borrower, and in that ordinary case it is connected to the positive command of return. Scripture thereby revealed that an unlawful taking under this prohibition can nevertheless create a valid pledge. Once the Torah reveals that principle for the borrower, it applies to the guarantor as well. Even though the guarantor is not personally subject to the return command, the Torah's treatment of this prohibition as one whose act remains effective extends to every application of the same prohibition. This is the reasoning explained above in seif katan 7. But this works only if the prohibition against taking a food implement is shared by both an ordinary borrower and a guarantor. If one were to say that the separate verse applies only to the guarantor, the original difficulty would return, because there would be no case within that prohibition where Scripture revealed through a positive command that the unlawful act remains effective. One could perhaps say, as Tosafot write in the passage beginning "he takes," that the Gemara in Temurah challenges Rava from ordinary practice. The present Gemara can similarly be understood as challenging from ordinary practice. We see that even with a guarantor the creditor does not have to return the pledge immediately. Why is that so? It must be because the special prohibition also applies to an ordinary borrower, where the Torah's return command reveals that the original taking remains legally effective. If so, the Gemara can properly ask why the special prohibition is needed for an ordinary borrower, since taking collateral is already prohibited there. This would resolve the matter. The difficulty is that the Ramah expressly holds that even a guarantor is subject to the return obligation in this context, so this particular reconciliation cannot be used. In any event, according to the Ramah, although Scripture excludes a guarantor from the prohibition on entering the debtor's house, it does not exclude him from the separate prohibition against taking a food preparation implement. The same should therefore be true of property taken for consecrated obligations or charity to the poor. There we say that the obligation of periodic return does not apply because Scripture says, "and it shall be righteousness for you," implying a private creditor to whom the act of return is credited. But that only excludes the positive command of return. The separate prohibition "he shall not take the millstones" has not been excluded. This is especially compelling because without the verse "and it shall be righteousness for you," we would have thought that even obligations of valuation require periodic return, through the verbal analogy of the word "assessment." If the Torah needed a special verse only to remove the return obligation, what basis is there to remove the independent prohibition against taking a food implement? Why should consecrated or charitable debts be more lenient than a guarantor? The Rama above, in seif 12, writes that this leniency applies specifically to food preparation implements, which at first glance sounds as though the collectors of consecrated or charitable funds may take even such items. That cannot be correct. Rather, the Rama must mean only that although taking the item is prohibited, it is not subject to periodic return because the positive command "you shall surely return it" does not apply there. The unlawful taking nevertheless remains legally effective for the same reason explained above regarding the guarantor: Scripture revealed within this prohibition that the act itself can take effect despite the transgression. The Rama's earlier statement must therefore concern only the absence of a return obligation, not permission to take the pledge initially.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
אלמנה וכתב הסמ"ע ה"ה גרושה והט"ז כתב ה"ה פנויה ועיין תומים כי ח"ו להוסיף ולשנות קוצו של יו"ד מהתורה דוקא אלמנה ולא אחרת זולתה:
שלא בשעת הלואה לאפוקי מדעת הרמב"ם דסבירא ליה דאף בעת הלואה אין ליקח ממנה משכון קמ"ל דלא דכל חבלה הכתוב בקרא היינו שלא בשעת הלואה ועיין תומים מ"ש בדברי הרמב"ם:
ואם וכו' בע"כ היינו בעת הצורך להחזיר ולא תיכף כמש"ל:
אם תודה תשלם ואם תכפור תשבע הקשה סמ"ע בממ"נ אם לית ליה עדים דלקחו ועדי ראה למה נאמנת בשבועה הא יש לו מגו דלהד"ם כדאמרי' להדיא בגמרא גבי חובל כלי אוכל נפש דאף דמחויב להחזיר מ"מ יש לו מגו דלהד"ם או החזרתי ואי איירי דאיכא עדי ראה ג"כ פשיטא דהיא נאמנת והש"ך הביא בשם ריב"ש תי' דה"א אלמנה הואיל וחס רחמנא עליה מבלי למשכנה א"כ ה"ה לכופה לתשלומין לא ומכ"ש שלא להטיל עליה שבועה בכפירתה קמ"ל דשוה דינה בשאר דברים לשאר בני אדם וצריכה לשלם וכופים אותה וכן אם נתחייבה שבועה אין הבדל והבעה"ת וגי"ת לא ס"ל פי' זה ברמב"ם ועיין תומים דכתבתי פי' רבים. ולדינא כולם אפשר ישרים וברורים ובפרט במ"ש בחובל אלמנה עשירה דאינו מחויב להחזיר לה דאינו נאמן דהחזיר דמהכי תיתי יחזיר כיון שאין עליו חיוב החזרה. וגם כתבתי דהוי ליה חשוד ואינו יכול לטעון טענת כך חייב לי במגו דהא צריך לישבע שבועת המשנה עיין שם כי הכל ברור לדינא ולא רציתי להעתיקו פעמיים:
אבד המשכון או נשרף וכו' לוקה ומחשב דמי משכון ששוה בחובו אפילו נאבד באונס הואיל וחבל שלא ברשות קנאו ונתחייב בו באונסין וכן הדין בחבל כלי אוכל נפש או כל אלמנה לדידן דאין אסור אלא שלא בעת הלואה ועיין תומים דכתבתי דאם אבדו או שרפו בידים נראה לומר דחייב ליקח כלי בדמיו וליתן למלוה לקיים העשה דהשבה ועיין שם מ"ש בישוב דברי הרמב"ם כי רבים חולקים וס"ל דאין כאן מלקות ולא נ"מ לדידן דלית לן מלקות בעו"ה וחשוד נעשה אפילו לית ביה מלקות דהא לאו דחמס הוא ופסול כנ"ל בסימן ל"ד ע"ש:
אבל לערב דכתיב לביתו ולא לבית ערב גמ' וברמב"ם נתן טעם דכתיב לקח בגדיו כי ערב זר והיינו משום דבקרא יש לומר לביתו למעט שכר שכיר וכדומה שלא היה הלואה מעולם אבל בערב דיש כאן הלואה אסור לכך עשו לו סמך מדברי קבלה לקח בגדיו וכו' וכיון דמוכח דקרא איירי בערב א"כ כ"ש בשכר שכיר כמ"ש דליכא כאן שום הלואה בעולם. והג"ת הניח הרמב"ם בצ"ע:
וי"א מ"מ וכו' דזהו לאו בפ"ע ואין בו מיעוט לערב ולפי דבריו ה"ה בחובל כלי אלמנה אם היא נעשית ערב דמ"ש דגם הוא לאו בפ"ע ועיין תומים שכתבתי דנראה דס"ל דבערב לית ביה מצות השבת עבוט דקרא השב תשיבם לא קאי עליה ומ"מ א"צ להחזיר תיכף אם חבל כלי אוכל נפש ולא אמרינן גביה אם עבד לא מהני ע"ש:
שלא למשכן כלי וכו' ועיין תומים דכתבתי דה"ה גזבר להקדש ולעניים הנזכר לעיל סעיף י"ב אף דליתא בהחזרה מ"מ א"י למשכן כלי אוכל נפש או כלי אלמנה רק אם חבלו אין צריך להחזיר כלל. ולכן יש להתבונן במה שנהגו בכמה קהלות ליטול משכנות בגין המס ונכנסים לבתי' וזהו אפשר דמותר דה"ל כמו גזבר או לביתו של ערב אבל במה דחובלים כלי אוכל נפש וכלי אלמנה יש לשים אל לב מי התיר להם זאת דאסור לכל. ודוחק דהם באין בשליחות של מלך לגבות מס המלך ודינו של מלכו חבול הכל וכמו שכתב הרא"ש בתשובה דנהיגי לתפוס גוף הלוה בשביל מס וג"כ הטעם משום דינא דמלכותא כו' צ"ע דלאו כל המסים לצורך המלך וגם אין לדמות האיסורים זה לזה דמי התיר זה בלי ראיה מוכרחת מש"ס ופוסקים. ובעו"ה הדבר נמסר לפרנסי הדור שהם על הרוב בני בלי בעלי תורה שאינם שואלים עצת בעלי הוראה וע"כ תצא בעו"ה משפט מעוקל וה' ירחם עמו להשיב שופטנו כבראשונה ויועצנו כבתחלה:
מותר למשכנו וכן אם גזלה שלו ביד חבירו אפילו אין הגזלה בעין רק שלא זקפו בהלואה מותר לכנס לבית חבירו למשכנו דהוי כמו שכר שכיר:
ואם זקף עליו השכר דאז נעשית מלוה ועיין לעיל סימן ס"ז מהו נקרא זקיפה ע"ש סעיף י"ד ומ"ש שם:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
A widow. Sema writes that the same applies to a divorced woman, and Taz writes that it applies even to an unmarried woman. See Tumim. Heaven forbid that one add to or alter even the smallest point of the Torah's wording. The prohibition applies specifically to a widow and to no other woman.
Not at the time of the loan. This excludes Rambam's view that even at the time of the loan one may not take collateral from her. The ruling teaches otherwise, because every 'taking of collateral' mentioned in the verse refers to taking it after the loan. See Tumim for what I wrote regarding Rambam.
And if, etc. Necessarily this refers to the time when the creditor would otherwise be required to return the collateral, not immediately after taking it, as explained above.
If she admits, she pays, and if she denies, she swears. Sema asks: if the creditor lacks witnesses that he took the collateral and witnesses who later saw it in his possession, why is the widow believed merely by swearing? The creditor has a migo that he could have denied taking it altogether, as the Gemara says explicitly concerning one who took a food preparation utensil as collateral. Even though he must return it, he has a migo that he could have said, 'It never happened,' or, 'I returned it.' If there are witnesses who saw it as well, then it is obvious that she is believed. Shach cites Rivash's answer: one might have thought that because the Torah had special compassion for a widow and prohibited taking collateral from her, the creditor likewise may not compel payment from her, and certainly may not impose an oath when she denies the debt. The ruling therefore teaches that in all other respects her law is the same as anyone else's. If she owes money she must pay and may be compelled, and if she incurs an oath obligation there is no distinction. Baal HaTerumos and Gidulei Terumah do not explain Rambam this way. See Tumim, where I gave several explanations. All may be correct in practical law. In particular, I wrote that one who took collateral from a wealthy widow and is not required to return it is not believed to say that he returned it, for why should we assume that he returned it when he had no obligation to do so? I also wrote that because he becomes disqualified from swearing through the transgression, he cannot claim, 'She owes me this amount,' through a migo, for he would need to take a Mishnah oath. See there, where the practical law is clear.
If the collateral was lost or burned, etc. He receives lashes and the value of the collateral is credited against the debt even if it was lost through an unavoidable accident. Since he took it unlawfully, he acquired responsibility for it and becomes liable even for accidents. The same applies where he unlawfully takes food preparation utensils or collateral from any widow, according to our ruling that the prohibition applies only after the loan. See Tumim. I wrote that if he himself destroyed or burned the collateral, there is reason to say that he must purchase a replacement utensil with his money and give it to the borrower in order to fulfill the positive commandment of return. See there for my reconciliation of Rambam. Many authorities disagree and hold that there are no lashes. This has no practical difference for us today, when lashes are not administered due to our sins. He nevertheless becomes disqualified even if there are no lashes, because this is a prohibition involving wrongful taking, as explained above in siman 34.
But from a guarantor. Scripture says 'his house,' excluding the house of a guarantor. Rambam gives an additional reason from the verse, 'Take his garment, for he guaranteed a stranger.' This is because one might otherwise interpret 'his house' as excluding wages and similar obligations that never arose from a loan. A guarantor, however, is connected to a loan, and one might think the prohibition applies. Therefore Scripture provides an allusion that even a guarantor is excluded. Once the verse is shown to exclude a guarantor, certainly wages and similar obligations that involve no loan at all are excluded. Gidulei Terumah nevertheless leaves Rambam difficult.
And some say nevertheless, etc. They hold that the prohibition concerning food preparation utensils is a separate prohibition and contains no exclusion for a guarantor. According to them, the same would apply to taking a widow's utensil where she became a guarantor, because that too is a separate prohibition. See Tumim. I wrote that this opinion appears to hold that the positive commandment to return collateral does not apply to a guarantor, because the verse 'you shall surely return it' does not refer to him. Nevertheless, if the creditor unlawfully took a food preparation utensil from a guarantor, he need not return it immediately on the ground that an unlawful act cannot take legal effect. See there.
Not to take a utensil, etc. See Tumim. I wrote that the same applies to a treasurer collecting for consecrated property or for the poor, mentioned above in seif 12. Although the requirement to return collateral does not apply to him, he may not take food preparation utensils or a widow's utensils. If he did take them, however, he need not return them. This requires reflection regarding the practice in some communities of taking collateral for taxes and entering homes. Entry may perhaps be permitted because the collector resembles a treasurer, or because this resembles entering the house of a guarantor. But the practice of taking food preparation utensils and a widow's utensils deserves serious attention. Who permitted what the Torah forbids to everyone? It is strained to say that the collectors act as agents of the king to collect royal taxes, and that royal law allows all property to be seized, comparable to Rosh's responsum permitting seizure of the debtor's person for taxes under the law of the kingdom. Not all taxes are for the king personally, and one cannot compare separate Torah prohibitions without a compelling source in the Gemara and authorities. Due to our sins, these matters are often entrusted to communal leaders who are not learned in Torah and do not seek the guidance of halachic authorities. Distorted judgment therefore results. May Hashem have mercy upon His people and restore our judges as at first and our advisers as at the beginning.
It is permitted to take collateral from him. Likewise, if another person holds property that he stole from him, even if the original stolen object is no longer present, provided the obligation has not been formally converted into a loan, he may enter the other's house and take collateral, for this resembles unpaid wages.
And if he converted the wages into a loan. Then it becomes a loan obligation. See above, siman 67 seif 14, regarding what constitutes such conversion and what I wrote there.

mechaber.he: יש מי שאומר שאין שליח ב"ד אסור ליכנס לביתו למשכנו אלא במשכנו להיות בטוח ממעותיו ולא הגיע זמן הפרעון אבל כשהגיע זמן הפרעון ובא לגבות חובו וזה אינו רוצה לפורעו והוא בחזקה שיש לו מטלטלין ומבריחם שליח ב"ד נכנס לביתו למשכנו ויפרע לזה חובו שפריעת ב"ח מצוה ומכין אותו עד שתצא נפשו כדי לקיימה אבל אין כופין אותו להשכיר עצמו ולא לעשות שום מלאכה כדי לפרוע ואפילו התנה על עצמו שיתפוש המלוה את גופו וכתב לו זה בשטר אינו מועיל ואינו יכול לא לאסרו ולא להשתעבד בו: הגה ודוקא שאין לו לשלם אבל אם יש לו ואינו רוצה לשלם ב"ד חובשין אותו ומכין אותו עד שתצא נפשו וכופין אותו לשלם (ד"ע באגודה פ' כל כתבי וריב"ש סי' תפ"ד וכמ"ש הטור) וי"א דאפי' אם אין לו לשלם אם ישבע להיות חבוש עד שישלם צריך לקיים שבועתו (ריב"ש סי' תפ"ד) ועיין לקמן סוף הסימן:
mechaber.en: Some say an agent of beit din is forbidden to enter the debtor's house to take collateral only when the seizure is intended to secure payment before the debt has fallen due. But when the due date has arrived, the creditor seeks to collect, the debtor refuses to pay, and it is presumed that he owns movable property which he is concealing, an agent of beit din may enter his house, seize collateral, and pay this person's debt. Repaying a creditor is a mitzvah, and the debtor is beaten until his soul departs in order to compel its fulfillment. He is not compelled, however, to hire himself out or perform labor in order to pay. Even if he stipulated that the lender could seize his body and wrote this in the document, the stipulation is ineffective; the lender may neither imprison him nor enslave him. {Rama: This applies when he lacks the means to pay. If he has the means but refuses, beit din imprisons and beats him until his soul departs and compels him to pay. Some say that even if he lacks the means, if he swore to remain imprisoned until he pays, he must fulfill his oath. See Rivash 484, note 90, and below at the end of this siman.}

baer_hetev.he:
להשכיר. נראה דהוא מטעם דכתיב כי לי בני ישראל עבדים שטר דהש"י הוא קודם ודוקא בגנב משל חבירו כתיב ונמכר בגנבתו ולא בהלואתו דלהוצאה נתנה ועמ"ש הטור בסי' צ"ט סי"ח וי"ט. סמ"ע:
ודוקא. עיין בתשובת ראנ"ח סי' נ"ח ובתשובת מהרשד"ם סי' ש"צ:
baer_hetev.en:
Renting. It seems that the children of Israel are slaves who have not yet been cursed before, and that they will be sold in their theft and not in the midst of Hashem’s curse, and the people of the High Court. A:
And Durk. See the response of the R.C. and the answer from the radar

beer_hagolah.he:
טור סכ"ח בשם ר"ח כן כתב הרא"ש אהא דאמר שמואל שליח בית דין מנתח נתוחי וכו' כתב תימה ואם לא ימצאנו בידו היאך יכפיהו לפרוע מצותו ואנן קיימא לן פריעת ב"ח מצוה וכו' ולפי' ר"ת ניחא וכו'
פי' לאפוקי כשאינו רוצה לגבות חובות עתה מאיזה טעם שיש לו ורוצה למשכנו הכל ולהחזיר לו קצת לעת צרכה ויהיה הכל משועבד לחובו דאז אפילו כבר הגיע הזמן אסור לשליח בית דין ליכנס לביתו סמ"ע
שם ס"ל כ"כ הרא"ש בתשובות כלל ע"ט שכ"כ ר"ת בתשובה:
שם בשם תשובת אביו הרא"ש כלל ס"ח סי' ז' וכ"כ הרשב"א בתשובה סי' אלף וס"ט וכן כתב הריב"ש ומ"ש בשם ספר אגודה דחובשין אותו והביא ראיה מדאמרינן דאבא בר מרתא הוא מסקי ביה זוזי בי ר"ג וכו' שבת דף קכ"א ע"ב איכא למימר דהוי עבדי דר"ג דהוי פריצי כדאיתא בפרק מי שאחזו (גיטין דף ס"ז ע"ב) ובשאר דוכתי
beer_hagolah.en:
Tur, seif 28, in the name of Rabbenu Chananel. The Rosh writes similarly regarding Shmuel's statement that an agent of beit din may seize an item outside the house, etc. He writes: This is difficult, for if he does not find the item in his hand, how can he compel him to pay his debt? Payment of a creditor is a mitzvah, etc. According to Rabbenu Tam's explanation, however, the matter is resolved, etc.
P. Lapochi, when he wants to back debts now from what point he has and wants to bring him back a bit to his soft time, and he will be all enslaved to his heart even now, the time must not be sent to his house
There, seif 30. The Rosh likewise writes in Responsa, rule 79, that Rabbenu Tam wrote this in a responsum.
There, in the name of a responsum of his father, the Rosh, rule 68, siman 7. Rashba likewise writes in Responsa siman 1069, and so writes Rivash. As for what is cited in the name of Sefer Agudah, that one may imprison him, with proof from the incident in which Abba bar Marta owed money to the house of Rabban Gamliel, etc., Shabbat 121b, one may answer that those were servants of Rabban Gamliel, who were forceful men, as stated in Gittin 67b and elsewhere.

beur_hagra.he:
יש מי. עבה"ג. דע"כ מתני' לא איירי בשעת פרעון דאל"כ מה חזרה שייך כיון דמסדרין וכמ"ש תוס' שם קי"ד א' ד"ה מה ערכין שאין כו':
שפריעת כו'. כתובות פ' הכותב (כתובות פ"ו א)':
אבל אין. כמ"ש בקדושין י"ח א' בגניבתו ולא כו' ועבכתובות ס"ג א' בתוס' ד"ה באומר כו' וכאן אפי' ר' אליהו מודה הרא"ש בת' ועסמ"ע וכ"ש לפיר"ת וראיה לדבריו ממ"ש שם באומר איני כו' ול"ק באין לו לזון:
ואפי' התנה. שם נ"ו א' ושאר מקורות בש"ס האומר לאשה כו' ואף לר' יהודה בדבר שבגוף מודה:
ב"ד חובשין. מ"ק פ"ג ומנלן דכפתינן כו'. ובפ' כל כתבי (שבת קכ"א ב)' שחשדוהו דה"ל במה לפרעו א"ל צורבא מרבנן כו' ולא משקר:
ומכין. כנ"ל:
וי"א דאפי'. שבועות כ"ז א' אביא נשבע להרע כו' ואמרי' בב"ק צ"א ב' דמ"ד אין רשאי לחבול כר"א הקפר כו' ומ"מ חייב לקיים נזירותו:
beur_hagra.en:
There is an authority... See Beer HaGolah. The Mishnah cannot be discussing actual collection when the debt is due, because then the law would be arrangement of the debtor's needs, not return of collateral. Tosafos 114a makes this point.
Payment of a debt... Kesubos, Perek HaKosev, 86a.
But one does not... Kiddushin 18a says "for his theft," excluding other debts. See Tosafos, Kesubos 63a. Even Rabbi Eliyahu concedes here, as the Rosh writes in a responsum, and all the more according to Rabbeinu Tam.
And even if he stipulated. Kesubos 56a and many other places teach that a stipulation cannot remove a Torah obligation concerning one's body. Rabbi Yehudah agrees in such a matter.
Beit din incarcerates him. Moed Katan, chapter three, derives that beit din may restrain a litigant. Shabbos likewise discusses a scholar suspected of falsely claiming inability to pay, with the assumption that a Torah scholar will not lie.
And they strike him. As above.
And some say that even... Shevuos 27a discusses an oath to harm oneself, and Bava Kamma 91b treats self-injury as prohibited according to Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, yet one who vowed nezirus remains obligated to observe it. The same principle applies here.

meirat_einayim.he:
אלא במשכנו להיות בטוח במעותיו ולא הגיע הזמן וה"ה אע"פ שהגיע כבר זמן הפרעון כשאינו רוצה לגבות חובו ממנו עתה משום דא"כ צריך לסדר לו ואין בידו דהלוה כדי הסידור וכדי חובו ומ"ה רצה למשכנו הכל ולהחזיר לו קצת לעת צרכו ויהי' הכל משועבד לחובו וכמ"ש הטור והמחבר בסי"ו (וטעם זה כתבו המפרשים כמ"ש בפרישה סכ"א) או משאר טעם שיש לו ולא כמשמעות ע"ש דס"ל דדוקא בתוך הזמן איירי עיש:
אבל אין כופין אותו להשכיר כו'. נראה דהוא מטעם דכתי' כי לי בני ישראל עבדים שטר דהש"י הוא קודם ודוקא בגנב משל חבירו כתי' ונמכר בגניבתו ולא בהלואתו שלהוצאה ניתנה ועמ"ש הטור בסי' צ"ח סי"ח וי"ט:
meirat_einayim.en:
But we continue to be confident in His words, and not the time has come, and He has not yet come to Him, and He has not made His hand in order to provide His covenant with Him, and He has not done so much to Him, and He has not done so much to Him
But there is no denying him to rent him. It seems that the children of Israel are slaves who have not yet been desecrated, and who are a thief of his duty, and who is sold in his theft and not in the loan of the expenditure given and the people of the CPA

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he: להיות בטוח. דהיינו בתו"ז כשרואין שמבזבז שלו או כשהגיע הזמן וא"ר להתפרע רק שרוצה למשכנו סמ"ע:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en: Be sure. This is to say that his daughter, when he is intoxicated, or when he comes to time, will only be disturbed by his son:

pitchei_teshuva.he:
שפריעת ב"ח מצוה. עיין בספר ארעא דרבנן בהשמטות אות קע"ז שכתב לפי דברי הרא"ש בתשובה שהביא מרן הב"י ביו"ד סימן רל"ח על מי שנשבע שלא למכור משלו לפרוע נראה דס"ל דהוא מצוה מדאורייתא ולא חלה עליה שבועה וכ"כ המבי"ט ח"א סימן נ"א ע"פ מ"ש רש"י בפרק הכותב דנפקא לן מדכתיב הן צדק ודרז"ל שיהא הן שלך צדק ואיכא למידק דלכאורה נראה דאינו אלא אסמכתא דפשטיה דקרא במדות הוא דכתיב וכ"כ מדברי רש"י בפרק מי שהיה נשוי בעובדא דקטינא דארעא דיתמי ושמא התם שאני דאיירי ביתמי שאינו אלא מפני כבוד אביהם אבל הלוה גופיה מצוה דאורייתא הוי והמבי"ט שם הביא בשם הרשב"ץ דנפיק מקרא דוהאיש אשר אתה נושה בו וכ"כ הרמב"ן בשלהי בתרא עכ"ל:
אין כופין אותו להשכיר. עבה"ט ועי' בס' שער משפט לענין אם החיוב מוטל עליו בעצמו להשכיר את עצמו והאריך בזה ומסיק וכתב וז"ל זאת תורת העולה מדברינו דנלע"ד דאף שלכ"ע אין ב"ד כופין אותו להשכיר עצמו כדי לפרוע חובו מ"מ לענין אם החיוב מוטל עליו בעצמו להשכיר עצמו לפרוע חובו תליא בפלוגתא דרבוותא דלשיטת התוספת אינו חייב כלל להשכיר א"ע לפרוע חובו אבל לשיטת הגמ"ר בשם מוהר"ם שהיא ג"כ שיטת הרמ"א ז"ל בסימן של"ג אף דאין כופין אותו מ"מ חייב בעצמו להשכיר א"ע בכדי לפרוע חובו עכ"ל.
ואינו יכול לא לאסרו כו'. ע' בפלפולא חריפתא פ' איזהו נשך סימן ל"ח בהא דאיתא התם והאידנא דנקט כתבי הכי קנינא מיניה ושהינא כמה עידנין והדר חכרה מיניה שפיר דמי כדי שלא תנעול כו' כתב וז"ל מכאן נ"ל ראיה שראוי לתקן תקנות לפריעת בעל חוב מה שהוא שלא מן הדין כמו לתפוס גופו בתפיסה וכיוצא בזה ואע"פ שהוא חוב דעיסקא וכיוצא בזה שיש למלוה בזה ריוח אפ"ה שייך טעמא כדי שלא תנעול דלת כדאשכחן הכא כו' כנ"ל ע"ש. ובתומים סקי"ג כ' וז"ל ובזמננו פשט המנהג שחובשין ללוה כשאין לו לשלם ואין מוחה ואולי הכל בחזקת שמבריחים נכסים וצ"ע כי אין להם על מה שיסמוכו עכ"ל ועי' בעט"צ מענין תקנות בורח:
שפריעת ב"ח מצוה. עיין בספר ארעא דרבנן בהשמטות אות קע"ז שכתב לפי דברי הרא"ש בתשובה שהביא מרן הב"י ביו"ד סימן רל"ח על מי שנשבע שלא למכור משלו לפרוע נראה דס"ל דהוא מצוה מדאורייתא ולא חלה עליה שבועה וכ"כ המבי"ט ח"א סימן נ"א ע"פ מ"ש רש"י בפרק הכותב דנפקא לן מדכתיב הן צדק ודרז"ל שיהא הן שלך צדק ואיכא למידק דלכאורה נראה דאינו אלא אסמכתא דפשטיה דקרא במדות הוא דכתיב וכ"כ מדברי רש"י בפרק מי שהיה נשוי בעובדא דקטינא דארעא דיתמי ושמא התם שאני דאיירי ביתמי שאינו אלא מפני כבוד אביהם אבל הלוה גופיה מצוה דאורייתא הוי והמבי"ט שם הביא בשם הרשב"ץ דנפיק מקרא דוהאיש אשר אתה נושה בו וכ"כ הרמב"ן בשלהי בתרא עכ"ל:
אין כופין אותו להשכיר. עבה"ט ועי' בס' שער משפט לענין אם החיוב מוטל עליו בעצמו להשכיר את עצמו והאריך בזה ומסיק וכתב וז"ל זאת תורת העולה מדברינו דנלע"ד דאף שלכ"ע אין ב"ד כופין אותו להשכיר עצמו כדי לפרוע חובו מ"מ לענין אם החיוב מוטל עליו בעצמו להשכיר עצמו לפרוע חובו תליא בפלוגתא דרבוותא דלשיטת התוספת אינו חייב כלל להשכיר א"ע לפרוע חובו אבל לשיטת הגמ"ר בשם מוהר"ם שהיא ג"כ שיטת הרמ"א ז"ל בסימן של"ג אף דאין כופין אותו מ"מ חייב בעצמו להשכיר א"ע בכדי לפרוע חובו עכ"ל.
pitchei_teshuva.en:
For repayment to a creditor is a mitzvah. See Eretz DeRabbanan, addenda, letter 177, who writes that according to the responsum of the Rosh cited by Beit Yosef in Yoreh Deah, siman 238, concerning one who swore not to sell his own property in order to repay a debt, it appears that the Rosh holds repayment to a creditor to be a Torah mitzvah, and therefore such an oath does not take effect. Mabit, part 1, siman 51, likewise writes this based on Rashi in the chapter HaKotev. Although one can question whether that derivation is only an asmachta, perhaps the cases suggesting so concern heirs, who pay only out of honor for their father, whereas the borrower himself has a Torah obligation. Mabit cites Rashbatz as deriving the rule from the verse concerning the person from whom one demands payment, and the Ramban likewise writes so at the end of Bava Batra.
We do not compel him to hire himself out. See Baer Heitev and Shaar Mishpat. Shaar Mishpat concludes that although all agree beit din does not compel a debtor to hire himself out to repay his debt, whether he personally is obligated to do so depends on a dispute. According to Tosafot he has no such obligation. According to the Mordechai in the name of Maharam, which is also the Rama's view in siman 333, he is personally obligated to hire himself out even though beit din cannot compel him.
And he cannot imprison him, etc. See Pilpula Charifta, chapter Eizehu Neshech, siman 38. Concerning the Gemara's statement that nowadays they take a document of acquisition from him, wait some time, and then lease the property back to him, in order not to close the door before borrowers, he writes that this proves it is proper to enact measures for repayment of debts even beyond strict law, such as imprisoning the debtor and similar measures. Even where the debt arises from an iska or another arrangement from which the lender profits, the rationale of not closing the door before lenders still applies, as is evident there. See there. Tumim, seif katan 13, writes: "In our times the custom has spread to imprison a borrower when he cannot pay, and no one protests. Perhaps this is because all are presumed to conceal assets. This requires study, for there is no clear source on which to rely." See Ateret Tzvi regarding enactments concerning fugitives.
For repayment to a creditor is a mitzvah. See Eretz DeRabbanan, addenda, letter 177, who writes that according to the responsum of the Rosh cited by Beit Yosef in Yoreh Deah, siman 238, concerning one who swore not to sell his own property in order to repay a debt, it appears that the Rosh holds repayment to a creditor to be a Torah mitzvah, and therefore such an oath does not take effect. Mabit, part 1, siman 51, likewise writes this based on Rashi in the chapter HaKotev, who derives the obligation from the verse requiring one's "yes" to be righteous. One can question this, because at first glance that derivation appears only to be an asmachta, since the plain meaning of the verse concerns honest measures. This also appears from Rashi in the chapter Mi SheHaya Nasui, in the case of a small parcel of land belonging to orphans. Perhaps, however, that case is different because it concerns orphans, who are obligated only because of the honor of their father, whereas the borrower himself has a Torah mitzvah to repay. Mabit there cites Rashbatz as deriving the rule from the verse concerning the man from whom you demand payment, and the Ramban likewise writes so at the end of Bava Batra.
We do not compel him to hire himself out. See Baer Heitev and Shaar Mishpat regarding whether he himself is nevertheless obligated to hire himself out. Shaar Mishpat discusses this at length and concludes: "The rule emerging from our discussion is that although according to everyone beit din does not compel him to hire himself out in order to repay his debt, whether he personally is obligated to do so depends on a dispute among the authorities. According to Tosafot, he has no obligation at all to hire himself out in order to repay his debt. According to the Mordechai in the name of Maharam, which is also the position of the Rama in siman 333, although beit din does not compel him, he himself is obligated to hire himself out in order to repay his debt."

siftei_kohen.he:
יש מי שאומר כו'. וכן פסק בספר ב"ה ע"ש ועיין בתשו' ר"א ן' חיים סימן נ"ח:
ודוקא שאין לו לשלם כו'. עיין בא"א דף פ"ד ע"ב שהגיה וי"א דוקא שאין כו' וליתא ועבד"מ ובספרי ועיין בתשובת ר"א ן' חיים סי' נ"ח ועיין בתשובת מהרשד"ם סי' ש"ץ:
siftei_kohen.en:
“There is someone who says yes. “And then, in the book, I will see it as a sign.”
This applies specifically when he has no means with which to pay. See the Ateret Aharon, folio 84b, who emends the text to read, “Some say that this applies specifically when he has no means,” but this is incorrect. See the Darchei Moshe and my own work. See also Responsa Rabbi Eliyahu ibn Chaim, siman 58, and Responsa Maharashdam, siman 390. Cited cross-references in the source: 50, 300.

turei_zahav.he: (סל"ד) וא"כ נאמן לומר פרעתיך בהיסת במגו דהחזרתי [ק"ל] עכשיו נמי שמחזיר לו המשכון למלוה למה לא יהא נאמן לומר פרעתיך דהא לא נתן המשכון שלא יהא הלוה נ"ל פרעתיך אלא בשביל שימצא לגבות חובו ובמה נתבטל ממנו הזכות הראשון שיהא נאמן לומר פרעתי דהא כאן מיירי בחוב ע"פ דאי בכתב פשיטא שאינו נאמן לומר פרעתי בכל גווני מטעם דשטרך בידי מאי בעי ונראה דדעת הר"י ברצולי בזה מדאמר לו אל תחזיר לי המשכון אלא בעדים והוא בכלל זה גם לא ישלם לו המעות אלא בעדים דהא משכון במקום מעות קאי עכשיו:
turei_zahav.en: (Seif 34) “He is therefore believed to say, ‘I paid you,’ with a hesset oath, by virtue of a migo that he returned the pledge.” This is difficult. Even now, when he returns the pledge to the lender, why should he not be believed to say, “I paid you”? The pledge was not given to prevent the borrower from claiming payment, but so that the lender would have a means of collecting the debt. By returning it, why should the borrower lose his original right to claim that he paid? The case must concern an oral debt, because with a written note he obviously cannot claim payment while the note remains in the creditor’s possession. It appears that Rabbi Yehudah of Barcelona holds that when the borrower was told, “Do not return the pledge except before witnesses,” this necessarily included, “Do not pay the money except before witnesses,” because the pledge now stands in place of the money.

urim_vetumim_tumim.he: ב"ד חובשין אותו ובתשובת רשב"א חולק ועיין בחדושי גרשוני שמביא ראיה מרש"י פסחים דף צ"א ד"ה בית אסורין של ישראל דפי' שם כגון לכופו להוציא אשה פסולה או לשלם ממון וכו' הרי דאף בזמן הבית היו חובשין אנשים אלמים לחבוש אותן עד שישלמו וכן כתב הרא"ש ורי"ף במ"ק מניין דעבדינן הרדפה היינו מקום צר שא"י לברוח. והרי הכל לפי עיני ב"ד ובזמננו פשוט המנהג שחובשין ללוה כשאין לו לשלם ואין מוחה ואולי הכל בחזקת שמבריחים נכסים וצ"ע כי אין להם על מי שיסמכו:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en: Beit din imprisons him. Responsa Rashba disagrees. See Chiddushei Gershuni, which brings proof from Rashi in Pesachim 91a, s.v. "a Jewish prison," where Rashi gives as examples imprisonment to compel a man to divorce a woman whom he is forbidden to keep, or to compel payment of money. This shows that even in the Temple era people who refused lawful payment could be imprisoned until they complied. The Rosh and Rif in Moed Katan likewise explain "pursuit" as confinement in a narrow place from which the person cannot escape. Thus everything depends upon the judgment of beit din. In our times the established practice is plainly to imprison a debtor who claims inability to pay, and no one protests. Perhaps the practice assumes that such debtors are concealing assets. Even so, the basis for an unqualified rule is not entirely clear and requires study.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
במשכנו להיות בטוח דאיירי בתוך זמנו ורואים שמבזבז שלו או בהגיע זמן ואין רוצה להתפרע מטעם שיש לו רק רוצה למשכנו לבטחון סמ"ע:

baer_hetev.he:
הכר. כ' הסמ"ע דלרבותא נקט כר בלילה דאע"פ שאינו צורך כ"כ שאפשר לו לישן על מצע ומפץ מ"מ במקום שרגילין בכר צריך להחזיר לו וכתב הש"ך דאין המלוה רשאי להשתמש בו בשעה שהוא בידו וכ"מ מדברי הרמב"ן בספר המלחמות ס"פ שבועת הדיינים ובחידושי הר"ן שם עכ"ל:
בניו. דמטלטלי דיתמי אינן משועבדים להמלוה מן הדין וזה שסיים אלא יפרע כו' דאל"כ קשה הלא גם בחיי הלוה יכול להפרע ממנו כשירצה להחזירו ע"ד שלא לחזור וליקח בתורת משכון וכמ"ש הט"ו בסכ"ג וגם לאחר תקנת הגאונים יש נ"מ בזה וכמ"ש בסי' ק"ז ע"ש. סמ"ע:
אינו. וכתב בד"מ סי' ע"ג סי"ט דמשמע מדברי המרדכי דלכ"ע דבר הצריך ללוה תדיר כגון כר ומחרישה צריך להמתין עד שפדאו עכ"ל ולפ"ז צ"ל דמ"ש שא"צ להחזיר ר"ל ומ"מ אינו יכול למכור שם:
רוצים. התוס' והרא"ש חולקין ע"ז עכ"ל סמ"ע עמ"ש לקמן ר"ס ק"ז דאינם חולקין. ש"ך:
baer_hetev.en:
The pillow. The Sema writes that a pillow at night is mentioned as a stronger example. Although it is not absolutely indispensable, since a person can sleep on bedding or a mat, in a place where people ordinarily use a pillow the creditor must return it. The Shach writes that the creditor may not use it while it is in his possession, as is implied by the Ramban in Milchamot at the end of Shevuat HaDayanim and by the Ran there.
His children. By strict law, movable property of orphans is not subject to their father's creditor. This explains the continuation, "rather, he shall collect," for otherwise the statement would be difficult. Even during the debtor's lifetime the creditor may collect from him whenever he wishes, provided that he returns the item not as collateral but as full payment, as stated in seif 23. Even after the enactment of the Geonim there remains a practical difference, as explained in siman 107. Sema.
Is not. Darkei Moshe, siman 73, seif 19, writes that the Mordechai implies that according to all opinions an item continually needed by the debtor, such as a pillow or plow, must remain until the debtor redeems it. Accordingly, when the text says that the creditor need not return it, this must mean that he nevertheless may not sell it. Sema.
Wish. Tosafot and the Rosh disagree with this. Sema. The Shach writes that, as he explains at the beginning of siman 107, they do not in fact disagree.

ketzot_hachoshen.he:
מדעת הלוה ע' מ"ש בסי' ע"ב סק"ב:
הכר בלילה. עש"ך סי' ע"ב ושם האריך בישוב השגת הרמב"ן על דעת רש"י ובעה"מ דס"ל דבע"ח קונה משכון להתחייב באונסין והקשה הא שואל כל הנאה שלו וזה המלו' אסור להשתמש ואם נשתמש מעלה שכר ללוה וכתב שם וז"ל ולפענ"ד אין מכל זה ראיה חדא מאן לימא לן שאין המלו' יכול להשתמש בשעה שהוא בידו כגון בכר ביום ובמחרישה בלילה כיון שהוא שלו לפרעון חובו אלא דרחמנא חייבי' לאהדורי ליה משום צדקה אבל כשהוא בידו יכול להשתמש וכו' א"כ אפי' תימא דאינו רשאי להשתמש אפ"ה חייב באונסין כיון דבע"ח קונה משכון הרי היא שלו לגמרי והא דאינו רשאי להשתמש בו היינו משום דכיון דרחמנא חייביה לעשות צדקה ולהחזירו בשעת תשמישו א"כ כשזה ישתמש יפחות מצדקה המוטלת עליו שיתקלקל ולא יוכל העני להשתמש בו זמן שהיה משתמש בו מקודם אבל מ"מ גוף המשכון שלו עכ"ל ע"ש וקשה בהא דאמרינן ס"פ המקבל תנו רבנן ואם איש עני הוא לא תשכב בעבוטו הא עשיר שכיב ופריך מאי קאמר רב ששת הכי קאמר ואם איש עני לא תשכב ועבוטו אצלך ופירש"י מאי קאמר וכי בשביל שהוא עשיר התירו לשכוב על טליתו והרי הוא כרבית אצלו שישתמש במשכנו חנם ע"כ ולפמ"ש הש"ך לא הוי פריך מידי דכיון דקונה משכון ושלו הוא והא דאינו רשאי להשתמש רק לקיים מצות צדק' להשיב אל העני בשלימות בלי קילקול וכיון דלעשיר ליכא מצות השבת העבוט ממילא יכול לשכוב על עבוטו א"ו כיון דגם בעשיר אינו רשאי להשתמש ע"כ מוכח דלא קנה כלל להשתמש בו:
שמתן שכר' בצדה והוא מתשובת הרמב"ן וק"ל דהא התוס' כתבו בפ"ק דבתרא דף ח' הא דכופין על מצות צדקה אע"פ שמתן שכר' בצדה משום דכתיב ביה נמי לאו דלא תאמץ ולא תקפוץ וע' ב"י בי"ד סי' רמ"ח שכתב כן בשם פוסקים ומכללם הרמב"ן וא"כ ה"נ איכא לאו דכתיב לא תשכב ועבוטו אצלך וכ"כ הרמב"ם פ"ג ממלוה עבר ולא השיב עובר בל"ת שנאמר לא תשכב בעבוטו ע"ש ואע"ג דאין לוקין על לאו זה דה"ל לאו שאין בו מעשה וכמ"ש הה"מ שם הא בצדקה נמי הוי לאו שאין בו מעשה ואפשר דהך תשוב' דהרשב"א הוא והרשב"א אפשר דס"ל דבצדקה נמי אין כופין אע"ג דאית ביה לאו וכנראה מדברי הב"י סי' רמ"ח שכתב בשם הרשב"א להקל בצדקה בכפי' וא"כ לדידן דכופין בצדקה כמבואר בש"ע סי' רמ"ח א"כ ה"ה בהשבת העבוט ונראה לענ"ד דהיכא דעבר ומשכנו שלא ברשות דאם לא קיים העשה שבה הרי הוא לוק' בזה ודאי ראוי לכל ב"ד מישראל אם יש לאל ידם לכוף כאגמון ראשו להחזיר ולקיים העשה שבה ואף ע"ג דמדברי הסמ"ע סקט"ו משמע דאפי' בכה"ג אין כופין מ"מ העיקר כמ"ש ורבים המתפרצים בזה מתקיפים לשלוח שלוחא בלי רשות ב"ד למשכן עבור חוב ואין מחזירין את הכר בלילה ולפמ"ש ראוי לכל ב"ד להשגיח על זה:
ketzot_hachoshen.en:
With the borrower's consent. See what I wrote in siman 72, seif katan 2.
The pillow at night. See the Shach in siman 72, where he discusses Ramban's objection to Rashi and Baal HaMaor, who hold that a creditor acquires a pledge to the extent of liability for accidents. Ramban asks: a borrower is liable for accidents because all benefit is his, whereas a creditor may not use the pledge and, if he does, must pay the borrower for that use. The Shach answers that this is not a proof. Who says the creditor may not use it when the pledge is in his hand, such as a pillow by day or a plow at night? Since it is his as security for payment, perhaps he may use it. The Torah requires him to return it to a poor debtor at the time the debtor needs it only as a charitable obligation. Even if use is forbidden, the creditor can still be liable for accidents because the pledge is fundamentally his; he may be barred from using it only because the Torah obligates him to return it intact for the poor person's use, and using it may wear it out and diminish that charitable return. This is difficult from the end of chapter HaMekabel. The baraita says, 'If he is a poor man, you shall not sleep with his pledge.' The Gemara asks: does that imply that if he is wealthy you may sleep with it? Rashi explains the question: why should a rich borrower's garment be permitted for the creditor's free use, which resembles interest? According to the Shach, there should be no difficulty. If the creditor acquires the pledge and the only bar to use is the mitzvah of returning it intact to the poor, then where the debtor is wealthy and there is no return obligation, the creditor should indeed be able to use it. The Gemara's assumption that he may not shows that the creditor does not acquire a right of use in the pledge.
Whose reward is stated alongside it. This comes from a responsum attributed to Ramban, but it is difficult. Tosafot in Bava Batra 8b says that although the reward for charity is expressly stated, we nevertheless compel charity because it also contains the negative commandments 'you shall not harden your heart' and 'you shall not close your hand.' Beit Yosef in Yoreh Deah siman 248 cites this in the name of the poskim, including Ramban. Here too, returning the pledge includes the negative command, 'you shall not sleep with his pledge,' and Rambam writes in chapter 3 of Hilchot Malveh that one who fails to return it violates that prohibition. Although no lashes apply because it is a prohibition without an action, the same is true of charity. Perhaps the responsum is actually Rashba's, and Rashba may hold that even charity is not compelled in the same manner despite the prohibition, as Beit Yosef's presentation in siman 248 appears to indicate. According to our ruling that charity is compelled, however, the same should apply to returning the pledge. In my opinion, where one unlawfully seized a pledge without authorization, failure to fulfill the positive command of returning it places the matter within the structure of a prohibition corrected by a positive command, and every Jewish beit din with power should certainly compel him forcefully to return it and fulfill the mitzvah. Although the Sema, seif katan 15, appears to imply otherwise, the principal law is as I have written. Many people breach this area by sending agents without beit din authority to seize property for debts and failing to return the debtor's pillow at night. Every beit din should supervise this carefully.

meirat_einayim.he:
את הכר בלילה כו'. הוא ל' המשנ' דתרי קראי כתיבי לא תשכב בעבוטו (פי' לא תשכב נפשך ועבוטו עדיין בידך) השב תשיב לו את העבוט כבוא השמש והיינו כסות לילה וכתי' עד בוא השמש תשיבנו לו והיינו כסות יום שמחזירו לידו כל היום עד שקיעת החמה דאז חוזר ונוטלו מידו ונקט כר בלילה לרבותא דאף על פי דאינו צורך כל כך שאפשר לו לישן על מצע ומפץ מ"מ במקום שרגילים בכר צריך להחזיר לו הכר:
ואת המחרישה ביום אע"פ שאינו כלי אוכל נפש דאזהר עליה התורה וכמ"ש הטור והמחבר לפני זה בס"ח מ"מ כיון שצריך לעשות בו מלאכ' להחיות נפשו והמחריש' הוא הכלי שע"י בא האוכל נפש צריך להחזירו לו וע' בסמוך סכ"ג:
ולא יעשה מטלטלין אצל בניו דמטלטלי דיתמי אינן משועבדין למלוה מן הדין וזה שסיים וכ' אלא יפרע מהמשכון אחר שמת הלוה דאל"כ קשה הלא גם בחיי הלוה יכול להפרע ממנו כשירצה להחזירו ע"ד שלא לחזור וליקח בתורת משכון וכמ"ש הטור והמחבר בסמוך בסכ"ב וגם לאחר תקנת הגאונים יש נ"מ בזה וכמ"ש בסי' ק"ז ע"ש:
אלא יפרע מהמשכון כו'. בטור מסיים בזה וכתב ז"ל וא"צ להחזירו לבניו ע"ש והמחבר כתבו בסמוך סעיף י"ט:
אינו חייב להחזיר. וכת' בד"מ סימן ע"ג סי"ט ומשמע מדברי המרדכי סוף המקבל דלכ"ע דבר הצריך ללוה תדיר כגון כר ומחריש' צריך להמתין עד שפדאו עכ"ל וצ"ל לפי זה דמ"ש א"צ להחזיר ר"ל אבל מ"מ אינו יכול למכור:
שמתן שכרה בצדה. דכתי' וברכך ולך תהיה צדקה לפני ה' אלהיך:
אבל אם רוצים לכוף כו'. התוס' והרא"ש חולקים ע"ז והארכתי מזה בדרישה בדרישה בר"ס ק"ז ועמ"ש שם בסמ"ע ועיין בי"ד ר"ס ר"מ:
meirat_einayim.en:
The pillow at night, etc. This is the Mishnah's language. Two verses are written: "You shall not sleep with his pledge," meaning your soul shall not sleep while his pledge remains in your possession, followed by, "You shall surely return the pledge to him when the sun comes," referring to nighttime clothing. Another verse says, "until the sun comes you shall return it to him," referring to daytime clothing, which he uses all day until sunset and then returns to the lender. A pillow is mentioned to teach that even though it is not absolutely indispensable, because one could sleep on a mat, where people ordinarily use a pillow it must be returned.
And the plow by day. Although a plow is not itself a food-preparation utensil expressly prohibited by the Torah, as explained in seif 8, since the borrower needs it for the work by which he earns his livelihood and it is the implement through which food is ultimately produced, it must be returned during the day.
It does not become ordinary movable property in the hands of his heirs. Under strict law, the movable property of orphans is not subject to a creditor's lien. Therefore the ruling concludes that after the borrower dies, the lender collects from the pledge. Otherwise, even during the borrower's lifetime he could collect from it whenever he wished by returning it not as a pledge but as payment. The rule remains relevant even after the enactment of the Geonim.
Rather, he collects from the pledge, etc. The Tur concludes that he need not return it to the borrower's children; the Mechaber states this below in seif 19.
He is not obligated to return it. Darkei Moshe implies from Mordechai that everyone agrees that an item the borrower needs constantly, such as a pillow or plow, may not be sold immediately and the lender must wait until the borrower redeems it. Thus "he need not return it" means he need not surrender possession permanently, but he still may not sell it.
Its reward is stated alongside it. The verse says, "He will bless you, and it shall be righteousness for you before Hashem your God."
But if they wish to compel, etc. Tosafos and the Rosh disagree. I discussed this at length in the beginning of siman 107 and in Yoreh Deah siman 240.

pitchei_teshuva.he:
אבל אם רוצים. עבה"ט ועיין בקצה"ח סק"ט וגם לקמן ר"ס ק"ז מ"ש בזה וע' בתשובת חתם סופר חח"מ סימן קע"ז שהאריך בענין זה:
אבל אם רוצים. עבה"ט ועיין בקצה"ח סק"ט וגם לקמן ר"ס ק"ז מ"ש בזה וע' בתשובת חתם סופר חח"מ סימן קע"ז שהאריך בענין זה:
pitchei_teshuva.en:
But if they wish. See Baer Heitev, Ketzot HaChoshen seif katan 9, and what is written below at the beginning of siman 107. Responsa Chatam Sofer, Choshen Mishpat, siman 177, discusses this matter at length.
But if they wish. See Baer Heitev, Ketzot HaChoshen, seif katan 9, and what I wrote below at the beginning of siman 107. See Responsa Chatam Sofer, Choshen Mishpat, siman 177, who discusses this matter at length.

siftei_kohen.he:
את הכר בלילה. בשעה שהוא ביד המלו' אינו רשאי המלו' להשתמש בו. וכן מוכח מדברי הרמב"ן בספר המלחמות ס"פ שבועת הדיינים ובחידושי הר"ן שם:
אבל אם רוצים לכוף התוס' והרא"ש חולקין עכ"ל סמ"ע ועמ"ש לקמן ר"ס ק"ז דאינן חולקין:
siftei_kohen.en:
The pillow at night. While it is in the creditor's possession, the creditor may not use it. This is also evident from Ramban's Sefer HaMilchamot at the end of the chapter Shevuat HaDayanim, and from the novellae of the Ran there.
