urim_vetumim_tumim.he:
הנדוניא ברשות' כו' משמע אפילו לכתובה יכולה לתפוס והדין זה צ"ע כי מהרי"ו תשו' ע"ח לא הביא ראיה כלל לדבריו ולא הבנתי הא היא מחויב' כל רגע ליתנ' לבעל דהא הם של בעל דנצ"ב הוא ובמעות לא שייך שבח בית אביה ואם כן הבעל שחייב לאחרים הא מוציאין מדר"נ ובתשובת הרא"ש כלל ל"ח סי' ב' דכתב באשה שהכניסה לבעלה תמור נדן שטר משכון על הקרקע והיה שטר ביד סופר וצוה הבעל קודם מותו להחזיר השטר לאשתו ובא ב"ח מוקדם שהיה על הבעל לגבות ממשכנת' וכתב הרא"ש דאין לו זכות בממ"נ דאם אמרינן דהוי כהכניס' לו קרקע הרי אין ב"ח גובה ואי הוא רק חוב בעלמא הרי הבעל יכול למחול ועוד כיון שהיא חייבת לבעל והבעל חייב לה כשימות ואם כן כשמת הרי מחזקת לפרעון ממה שתחת ידה וכו' עכ"ל הרי דוקא במת שהגיע זמן פרעון אבל בחיי' שאין כאן זמן פרעון ב"ח דבעל גובה כנראה להדיא מדברי הרא"ש בתשובה דאל"כ מה צורך לכל אריכות הלא לא הגיע מעולם ליד הבעל והרי היא מוחזק בהם ומה איריא דמת הבעל ובאמת מהרי"ו עשה שם בתשובה סניף דא"י לזונה וה"ל כמורד' ולא הפסידה נדן אבל באם יכול לפרנסה דיש לה נ"מ דפירי הם מספיקים או מעשה ידיה דין זה צל"ע שתהיה יכול לתפוס בכתוב' דלא ניתן לגבות מחיים ואין למהרי"ו ראיה כלל ותשוב' הרא"ש הנ"ל תיובתא:
ואפילו נשבה וכו' משמע הא כשנדוניא בידו דיכול לפדות עצמו ומזה הוכיח הרמ"א בתשובה סי' צ"ג דאין רשות ביד אשה לומר העמד ערב על נדוניא ויפה דייק אלא שיש להבין הא דלא ניתנה כתובה לגבות מחיי' הוא משום דה"ל תוך זמנו והא פסק לעיל בסי' ע"ג במבזבז נכסיו דיכול לעקלם אפילו תוך זמן ולדברי מהרש"ל כמש"ל דוקא מבזבז במרד ומעל והוא עושה שלא כהוגן אף אנו עושין עמו חוץ לדין לעקל תוך זמן אבל ביורד מטה מטה מבלי פשע אין לעקל לק"מ דהא אין לך אונס יותר מזה אבל להחולקים על מהרש"ל צ"ל דוקא בחוב דברור שיגיע זמן לפרעון אבל באשה יכול להיות שלא תבא לידי גבי' לעולם גם לא בריר ליה זמנו אימת יהי' וכי לעולם יעקלו לא שייך עיקול משא"כ לעיל דזמן קבוע וידוע וברור חיובו:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en:
The dowry is in her possession, etc. The wording implies that she may retain the dowry even toward payment of her ketubah. This ruling requires study. Mahari Weil, responsum 78, gives no proof for it. I do not understand how it can be correct, because every moment the wife is obligated to deliver these assets to her husband. They are his property as nichsei tzon barzel. With money there is no concept of retaining the specific ancestral property for the honor of her father's house. If the husband owes another creditor, the creditor should therefore be able to collect these assets through the rule of Rabbi Natan. The responsum of the Rosh, rule 38, siman 2, concerns a woman who brought into the marriage, in place of a cash dowry, a mortgage document on land. The document was held by a scribe. Before his death the husband directed that the document be returned to his wife. An earlier creditor of the husband sought to collect from that mortgage. The Rosh writes that the creditor has no right to it either way. If the arrangement is treated as though she brought actual land into the marriage, a creditor of the husband cannot collect it. If it is merely an ordinary debt, the husband could have forgiven it. Moreover, because she owes the husband the dowry while the husband will owe her the ketubah when he dies, once he has died she may retain what is under her control toward payment of her claim. The Rosh's language shows that her right to retain the assets for the ketubah arises specifically upon the husband's death, when the time for payment arrives. During his lifetime, before the ketubah is collectible, the husband's creditor can apparently reach property that she presently owes him. Otherwise there would have been no need for the Rosh's lengthy analysis. The asset never came into the husband's physical possession and she remained its holder. If mere possession were enough, the husband's death would be irrelevant. Mahari Weil did add another factor in his responsum: the husband was unable to support her, which gave her a status resembling a wife in rebellion from whom the dowry was not forfeited. But where the husband can support her, for example because she has nichsei melog whose fruits are sufficient for her maintenance, or because her earnings support her, the rule that she may retain the dowry toward a ketubah that is not collectible during the marriage requires study. Mahari Weil provides no proof for such a proposition, and the Rosh's responsum appears to refute it.
Even if he was taken captive, etc. This implies that where the dowry is already in the husband's possession, he may use it to redeem himself. From here the Rama, in responsum 93, correctly proves that a wife cannot demand that her husband provide security for the value of her dowry. There is nevertheless a question. The reason a ketubah cannot be collected during the husband's lifetime is that its due date has not arrived. Yet above in siman 73 we rule that when a debtor is dissipating his assets, beit din may restrain those assets even before the debt's due date. According to the Maharshal's view explained there, this presents no difficulty. Maharshal limits early restraint to a debtor who maliciously and improperly squanders his assets. Because he acts wrongfully, beit din departs from the ordinary rule and freezes the property. A person who is simply declining financially through no fault of his own is not subject to such restraint. There is no greater involuntary misfortune than captivity. According to the authorities who disagree with Maharshal, however, one must distinguish differently. Early restraint applies to an ordinary debt whose liability will definitely mature at a fixed and known time. A ketubah may never become collectible at all, and even when it will, its due date is unknown. It would be impossible to immobilize the husband's property indefinitely on the possibility that the ketubah might eventually become due. That differs from the case above, where both the obligation and its maturity are certain.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
אבל בגדי שבת וכו' דאין דעתו להקנות להם לחלוטין רק שיהיה ברשותו ליתן להם להלבישם אבל הם שלו וב"ח גובה ונראה אם הבעל אומר שנתן להם במתנה גמורה נאמן דהא מגו דנותן להם עכשיו במתנה גמורה והא תו א"י ב"ח לגבות הימנו אם לא אם יש לב"ח מא"ק דאפשר אם נותן בזמן הסידור לאחר למתנה לא שייך תקנת שוק ולכ"ע ב"ח גובה ולית ליה מגו וצ"ע אבל זולת זה ודאי יש לו מגו דכל כמה דלא הגבהו לב"ח יכול ליתן מתנה ואין ב"ח מוציא ממנו. מיהו במרדכי פרק נערה שנתפתת' משמע דצריך שבועה וצ"ע הא יש לו מגו ואולי הוא למ"ד לא אמרינן מגו לפטור משבועה:
אם היה טבעות וכו' ובזה אף י"ח מודים דאין דרך להקנות במתנה אבל אם ידוע שנתן להם מתנה אפילו מטבעת אין לב"ח כלום ועיין בס"ק הקדום אם הבעל נאמן במגו:
היא נאמנת בטור כתב בשבועה דס"ל דהואיל דהם בחזקת הבעל הוי כנוטלת ולכך צריך שבוע' או די"ל דנשבעת היסת דמיירי דהבעל מכחיש דאל"כ בלא"ה נאמן במגו כמש"ל וא"כ ה"ל טענת ברי ע"פ הבעל:
אם עדיין הנדוניא וכו' עיין תומים שדין זה צ"ע ומיירי דוקא אם אין לה מזונות כלל ע"ש:
ואפילו נשבה וכו' אבל אם בידו יכול לפדות עצמו ואין האשה יכול' לעכב שמאבד כתוב' ונדוניא שלה ועיין תומים:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
But Shabbos clothing, etc. His intent is not to transfer ownership of these garments to them absolutely. Rather, they remain his property, with permission for him to give them to his family members to wear. Therefore a creditor may collect from them. It appears that if the husband says that he gave the garments to them as an absolute gift, he is believed, for he has a migo that he could give them an absolute gift now, in which case the creditor could no longer collect them. This may not apply where the creditor has a lien on movable property together with land, for perhaps the market protection enactment does not apply to a gift made to another at the time of arranging the debtor's necessities, and according to all opinions the creditor could then collect, leaving no migo. This requires study. Aside from that case, he certainly has a migo, because until the property is actually delivered to the creditor he may give it away, and the creditor cannot recover it from the recipient. Mordechai in the chapter Na'arah Shenispattah implies, however, that an oath is required. This requires study, for he has a migo. Perhaps Mordechai follows the opinion that a migo is not used to exempt from an oath.
If there were rings, etc. Here even the dissenting opinion agrees, because it is not ordinarily assumed that such articles were given as an absolute gift. But if it is known that he did give them as a gift, even if they are rings, the creditor has no claim to them. See the preceding seif katan concerning whether the husband is believed through a migo.
She is believed. Tur writes that she is believed with an oath, because he holds that since the articles are presumed to belong to the husband, she is considered one who collects from another and therefore requires an oath. Alternatively, she takes hesset where the husband denies her claim. Otherwise, he himself would be believed through the migo explained above, and therefore her definite claim rests upon the husband's statement.
If the dowry is still, etc. See Tumim. This ruling requires study and applies specifically where she has no right to support at all. See there.
Even if he was taken captive, etc. But if the money is in his possession, he may redeem himself with it, and the wife cannot prevent him on the ground that doing so diminishes her ketubah and dowry rights. See Tumim.

בכלל פרעון אף שבועתו לא חלה עליו כי לא נתכוון זה בשבועה אלא מה שהוא בכלל פרעון אבל בדבר שאינו בכלל פרעון לא על זה נדר או נשבע כלל ועיי' תשובת הרא"ש כלל ח' דין ד' דכתב דסתמא דמילתא דאין אדם נשבע למכור להדיא דמסדרין רק מ"מ י"ל בתשובה מספקא ליה כמ"ש הב"י דבב"מ כתב דעת ר"ת לבסוף וכן הטור בב"מ ברמזים כ' הדבר בספק אף דבנדרים כתב להדיא דמסדרין א"כ א"ש אך לפ"ז מוכח מזה כמש"ל בשבועה לא מ"ל קים ליה וספק שבועה לחומרא ועיין לעיל בכללי קים לי':
urim_vetumim_tumim.en: And he shall not violate his oath. This ruling is disputed. Rivash writes that where a person swore to pay a debt but has no means to do so, there is no greater circumstance beyond his control. What should he do, steal or rob in order to fulfill his oath? Rivash concludes that beit din nevertheless leaves him the protected minimum of property according to the order set out by the Rambam in chapter 2 of Hilchot Malveh for one who claims that he lacks the means to pay. This is explicit: the ordinary debtor's exemptions are preserved even though he swore. At first glance there is a clear proof for Rivash from the law of vows. Why should an oath be stricter than a vow? If a debtor must throw himself into destitution to fulfill his oath, then one who vows, "It is upon me to give one hundred to the Temple treasury," should likewise have to strip himself of all protected property in order to fulfill the vow. Yet we rule that those obligated by valuations and one who says "one hundred is upon me for the Temple treasury" are given the standard protected allowance, as stated in the Gemara and codified by the Rambam in Hilchot Arachin, chapter 3. We do not say that he must impoverish himself to fulfill his vow. Surely a private creditor should not have greater rights than consecrated property. One might distinguish that where a person swore merely to pay without fixing a date, beit din can preserve the protected minimum because he may yet fulfill the oath later. But if he fixed a date, once that date passes he violates the oath, and perhaps he must therefore impoverish himself in order to pay on time. This distinction is strained. Neither the Shulchan Aruch nor the responsum Chazeh HaTenufah, which is the source of the present ruling, makes any distinction between an oath with a fixed date and one without. Moreover, when no date is stated, every moment can itself be considered a time when performance is due. It therefore appears that Rivash is correct as practical law. Once Torah law itself establishes that certain basic assets are not included in ordinary debt collection, the debtor's oath to pay is naturally understood as an oath to perform what legally counts as payment. He did not intend to include property that Torah law removes from the collection process. The responsum of the Rosh, rule 8, law 4, similarly writes that ordinarily a person who swears to pay is not understood to have sworn to sell every possession, sleep in the street, and die of hunger. This is precisely the rationale of the debtor's protected minimum. The oath attaches only to assets legally included in payment. That conclusion is simple if it is certain that the debtor is entitled to the protected allowance. But there is an old dispute whether such an allowance exists in ordinary debt collection. Rabbenu Tam rules that the halachah follows the authority who gives the debtor no such allowance. The Rashba writes that even if a protected allowance applies when taking collateral, it may not apply to actual payment. Asifat Zekenim cites the Rashba and concludes that Rabbenu Tam's position would have appeared correct, were it not that the words of the Geonim are received tradition and should be followed, particularly because money should not be extracted without clear proof. Thus the matter was treated as sufficiently doubtful to prevent collection. Accordingly, Chazeh HaTenufah may have been uncertain on the underlying monetary law and inclined toward Rabbenu Tam, while nevertheless refusing to remove property because of the doubt. That restraint works for monetary law, but an oath raises a possible Torah prohibition, and in a doubt of Torah prohibition we are stringent. If perhaps the halachah is that there is no protected allowance, then those assets are legally included in payment and the oath attaches to them. The debtor would then have to impoverish himself in order to avoid a possible violation of a Torah oath. There is no contradiction from vows to the Temple treasury. There the law of the protected allowance is certain and explicit. The entire doubt is whether ordinary creditors are learned from the law of consecrated valuations. Since sacred obligations themselves unquestionably preserve the allowance, an oath or vow to pay them plainly does not extend beyond that legal obligation. Rivash, for his part, clearly rules like the Rambam and those who hold that ordinary creditors also must leave the debtor the protected minimum. It therefore follows directly that the oath does not attach to those exempt assets, just as a vow to the Temple treasury does not. This explanation is sound. It is true that Chazeh HaTenufah is traditionally attributed to the Rosh, and in Nedarim chapter 9 the Rosh expressly rules that the debtor is given the protected allowance. Still, the responsum may have treated the issue as doubtful, much as the Beit Yosef notes that in Bava Metzia the Rosh cites Rabbenu Tam's position last, and the Tur's abridged rulings there also leave the matter uncertain despite the explicit statement in Nedarim. On that basis the responsum can be reconciled. This reasoning also supports what I wrote above in the rules of kim li: in matters of oath, a litigant cannot simply invoke kim li to rely on the lenient monetary opinion, because a doubtful Torah oath is treated stringently. See there.
